title: What is Delta Live Tables (DLT) — a declarative ETL framework on Databricks for building and managing data pipelines with built-in data quality expectations (`EXPECT`), automatic dependency management, and pipeline monitoring — and how does it differ from Structured Streaming (DLT is higher-level, declarative, with quality checks; Structured Streaming is lower-level, imperative)?

s1_definition.profdef: Delta Live Tables is a declarative ETL framework on Databricks where you define the tables you want and the transformations that produce them, and the framework automatically works out the dependency order, manages the underlying Structured Streaming or batch execution, enforces data-quality rules declared with expectations, and provides built-in monitoring and recovery. It differs from Structured Streaming in that Structured Streaming is a lower-level, imperative API where you manually write and wire each stream, manage checkpoints, and handle quality and orchestration yourself, whereas Delta Live Tables raises the abstraction so you declare the what and the framework handles the how.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank of India needs a multi-step assembly line that turns raw trade records into clean records and then into a fraud report. With Structured Streaming you are the factory engineer who personally builds each conveyor belt, wires the motors, decides the order belts run in, installs the quality inspectors, and keeps restarting belts when they jam. With Delta Live Tables you instead write a simple blueprint saying raw feeds into clean, clean feeds into the fraud report, and here are the quality rules each stage must pass, and the framework builds the conveyor belts, figures out the correct order automatically, installs the inspectors, runs it, and self-heals when something jams. You describe the destination; the framework lays the track.
s1_definition.oneliner: Delta Live Tables is declarative ETL where you define tables, transformations, and quality expectations, and the framework auto-manages dependencies, execution, and monitoring, while Structured Streaming is the lower-level imperative engine you would otherwise wire by hand.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Delta Live Tables is a declarative ETL framework on Databricks where you define the tables you want and the transformations that produce them, and the framework automatically works out the dependency order, manages the underlying Structured Streaming or batch execution, enforces data-quality rules declared with expectations, and provides built-in monitoring and recovery. It differs from Structured Streaming in that Structured Streaming is a lower-level, imperative API where you manually write and wire each stream, manage checkpoints, and handle quality and orchestration yourself, whereas Delta Live Tables raises the abstraction so you declare the what and the framework handles the how.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine the National Bank of India needs a multi-step assembly line that turns raw trade records into clean records and then into a fraud report. With Structured Streaming you are the factory engineer who personally builds each conveyor belt, wires the motors, decides the order belts run in, installs the quality inspectors, and keeps restarting belts when they jam. With Delta Live Tables you instead write a simple blueprint saying raw feeds into clean, clean feeds into the fraud report, and here are the quality rules each stage must pass, and the framework builds the conveyor belts, figures out the correct order automatically, installs the inspectors, runs it, and self-heals when something jams. You describe the destination; the framework lays the track.

**One line to remember:** Delta Live Tables is declarative ETL where you define tables, transformations, and quality expectations, and the framework auto-manages dependencies, execution, and monitoring, while Structured Streaming is the lower-level imperative engine you would otherwise wire by hand.

sections.s2_technical:
Structured Streaming is powerful but low-level: for a multi-stage pipeline you write each stream yourself, set up each checkpoint, decide the execution order, add your own validation logic, and build your own orchestration and error handling. That gives full control but means a lot of boilerplate and operational code, and the correctness of dependency ordering and quality enforcement is on you. Delta Live Tables sits on top of this. You write a set of table or view definitions, each decorated to say what it is, for example in Python `@dlt.table` on a function that returns a DataFrame, and inside you reference other DLT tables with `dlt.read` or `dlt.read_stream`. From those references, Delta Live Tables builds a dependency graph automatically and runs the tables in the correct topological order, so you never manually sequence stages. It manages the Structured Streaming machinery underneath, including checkpoints and incremental processing, so you do not hand-wire them.

The defining feature is data-quality expectations. You attach declarative rules to a table with constructs like `@dlt.expect("valid_amount", "amount > 0")`, and Delta Live Tables enforces them with a choice of actions: `expect` keeps bad rows but records the violation as a metric, `expect_or_drop` drops rows that fail, and `expect_or_fail` stops the pipeline on violation. These expectations are first-class, tracked, and surfaced in the pipeline UI, so data quality becomes part of the pipeline definition rather than ad hoc code, and you get automatic metrics on how many rows passed or failed each rule. Delta Live Tables also provides built-in monitoring with a visual lineage graph of the tables, run history, and data-quality dashboards, and it handles operational concerns like automatic retries and recovery, so a transient failure does not require manual intervention.

Delta Live Tables supports both streaming tables, which process data incrementally as it arrives, and materialized views, which recompute results, and it underpins the medallion architecture naturally: bronze, silver, and gold tables are just DLT tables that read from one another, each rebuildable from the layer below. It also integrates Auto Loader for ingestion and supports change data capture through apply-changes. A senior-level nuance is positioning: Structured Streaming is the engine and the right tool when you need fine-grained control, custom stateful logic, or you are embedding streaming inside a larger application, while Delta Live Tables is the right tool when you want a maintainable, declarative, quality-governed pipeline without writing orchestration and checkpoint plumbing, and in fact Delta Live Tables uses Structured Streaming underneath. Another nuance is that Delta Live Tables is a managed Databricks feature, so it adds platform dependence, and it runs as its own pipeline with its own compute, which you configure for triggered or continuous execution. The practical rule is to reach for Delta Live Tables for standard multi-stage ETL where reliability, dependency management, and built-in quality matter, and to drop to Structured Streaming when you need low-level control that the declarative model does not expose.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At the National Bank of India, the trade data pipeline had three stages, raw ingestion, cleaning, and a fraud report, each written as a separate Structured Streaming job. Engineers had to manually ensure the cleaning job ran only after ingestion, wire a checkpoint for each, and bolt on their own validation code, and when the ordering or a checkpoint was misconfigured the pipeline produced wrong or partial data. This is exactly the problem Delta Live Tables solves: it works out the dependency order automatically and manages the streaming plumbing for you.

This is exactly how Delta Live Tables differs from Structured Streaming. Instead of hand-wiring three streams and their order, you declare three tables that read from each other, and the framework builds the dependency graph, runs them in order, and manages checkpoints.

Problem 2 — Data quality was enforced inconsistently, with validation scattered as if-statements, and bad rows like negative amounts sometimes slipped into the fraud report. Delta Live Tables expectations let you declare the quality rules on each table and choose to keep, drop, or fail on violations, with automatic metrics. This is the built-in quality capability.

Because we cannot run a real Delta Live Tables pipeline, this runnable demo models its declarative core. A `DltPipeline` registers table definitions with their dependencies and expectations, builds the dependency graph, and runs tables in topological order. An `Expectation` holds a rule and an action of keep, drop, or fail. A `DltTable` is a declared transformation. The demo declares bronze, silver, and gold trade tables with expectations, lets the framework resolve the order automatically, runs them, and shows rows dropped or kept by expectations with quality metrics, contrasting with the manual wiring Structured Streaming would require.

```yaml
# application.yml
dlt:
  pipeline-name: trade_fraud_pipeline
  execution-mode: triggered        # triggered | continuous
  storage-location: /pipelines/trade_fraud
  tables:
    - bronze_raw
    - silver_clean
    - gold_fraud
```

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a landing source of four trade rows, two of which are bad, one with a negative amount and one with a blank account, and three table definitions declared deliberately out of order.

Step 1: The pipeline resolves the dependency order from the declared dependencies alone. Even though gold was declared first, the framework sees gold depends on silver, silver depends on bronze, and bronze depends on landing, so it orders them bronze, then silver, then gold, with no manual sequencing.

Step 2: The bronze table reads the landing source and passes rows through. Its expectation that a trade id is present is set to keep, so all four rows stay in bronze, and the one with a blank account is still kept here because bronze only checks the trade id.

Step 3: The silver table reads bronze and applies two drop expectations. The positive amount rule drops the negative-amount row, and the valid account rule drops the blank-account row. So silver keeps only the two good rows, and the framework records that two rows passed and two failed.

Step 4: The gold table reads silver and keeps only high-value trades of seventy-five thousand or more. Of the two clean rows, one is fifty thousand and one is eighty thousand, so gold keeps the eighty-thousand trade, and its keep expectation records the metric.

Step 5: The pipeline completes having managed the ordering, the per-stage execution, and the quality enforcement automatically, and the final gold fraud output contains just the single high-value clean trade, with quality metrics available for each stage.

sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — DLT Framework Design ═══

  ┌─ Design Patterns Used ────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Declarative/Builder: DltTable declares intent, not execution      │
  │  Dependency resolution: topological sort of the table graph        │
  │  Strategy: Expectation.Action = KEEP / DROP / FAIL                 │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ SOLID Principles Applied ────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  S: Table declares transform; Pipeline orders+runs; Expectation QC │
  │  O: add a table or expectation without touching the runner         │
  │  D: Pipeline depends on DltTable/Expectation abstractions          │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── Class Diagram ──────────────────────────────────────────────────

  ┌──────────────┐        ┌──────────────────────┐
  │ DltPipeline   │◆──────▶│ DltTable              │ (pipeline owns tables)
  │ - tables      │        │ - name, dependsOn     │
  │ - sources     │        │ - transform           │
  │ + run()       │        │ - expectations[] ◆────┼──▶┌──────────────┐
  │ - resolveOrder│        │ + expect(Expectation) │   │ Expectation  │
  └──────────────┘        └──────────────────────┘   │ - rule, action│
                                                       │ + evaluate() │
                                                       └──────────────┘

  Contract for run:
    Pre:  tables declare valid dependsOn (acyclic)
    Post: tables executed in topological order; expectations enforced
    Guarantee: KEEP keeps+records, DROP removes, FAIL stops pipeline

  ── Call Chain (Main Scenario) ─────────────────────────────

  1. addSource("landing", 4 rows)
  2. table(gold), table(bronze), table(silver)  [any order]
  3. run() → resolveOrder() → [bronze, silver, gold]
  4. bronze: keep all 4
  5. silver: drop -5000, drop blank-account → 2
  6. gold: filter ≥ 75000 → 1 (TRD-3)
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Delta Live Tables is a declarative ETL framework on Databricks where you define the tables you want and the transformations that produce them, and the framework figures out the dependency order, manages the underlying execution, enforces data-quality rules, and gives you built-in monitoring and recovery. The contrast with Structured Streaming is the heart of the answer: Structured Streaming is the lower-level, imperative engine where you write each stream yourself, set up each checkpoint, decide the execution order, add your own validation, and build your own orchestration, which gives full control but a lot of plumbing. Delta Live Tables raises the abstraction so you declare the what, decorating functions as tables that read from one another, and the framework derives the dependency graph from those references, runs the tables in the correct order, and manages the Structured Streaming machinery, including checkpoints, underneath.

Its defining feature is data-quality expectations. You attach declarative rules to a table and choose an action: expect keeps bad rows but records the violation as a metric, expect or drop removes failing rows, and expect or fail stops the pipeline. These are first-class and tracked, so quality becomes part of the pipeline definition rather than scattered if-statements, and you get automatic pass and fail metrics per rule. On top of that, Delta Live Tables provides a visual lineage graph, run history, quality dashboards, and automatic retries, so a transient failure recovers without manual intervention. It supports streaming tables and materialized views, underpins the bronze-silver-gold medallion architecture naturally since each layer is just a table reading from the one below, and integrates Auto Loader and change data capture. The honest nuance is that it uses Structured Streaming underneath and is a managed Databricks feature, so Structured Streaming remains the right tool when you need fine-grained control or custom stateful logic, while Delta Live Tables is the right tool when you want a maintainable, quality-governed pipeline without writing orchestration and checkpoint code.

At the National Bank of India our trade pipeline had three stages written as separate Structured Streaming jobs, and engineers had to manually ensure cleaning ran after ingestion, wire a checkpoint for each, and bolt on validation, and misconfiguration occasionally produced wrong or partial data while bad rows like negative amounts slipped into the fraud report. We rewrote it in Delta Live Tables as three declared tables, bronze reading the landing feed, silver reading bronze, and gold reading silver, and the framework resolved the order automatically and managed the streaming plumbing. We moved the quality rules into expectations, dropping negative amounts and blank accounts at the silver stage with automatic metrics, so bad data no longer reached the report and the quality was visible in the pipeline UI. The result was far less operational code and a pipeline whose dependencies, execution, and data quality were all managed declaratively, which is exactly what Delta Live Tables is for.
